facts.fact_text: The United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden (also referred to as 'the applicant association' or 'Ilinden') is an association based in south-western Bulgaria.
Mr Boris Stankov is a Bulgarian citizen.
Mr Boris Stankov lives in Petrich.
At the relevant time Mr Boris Stankov was the chairman of a branch of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden.
The United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden was founded on 14 April 1990.
According to its statute and programme, the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden aimed to 'unite all Macedonians in Bulgaria on a regional and cultural basis'.
According to its statute and programme, the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden aimed to achieve 'the recognition of the Macedonian minority in Bulgaria'.
Section 8 of the statute of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden stated that the organisation would not infringe the territorial integrity of Bulgaria.
Section 9 of the statute of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden stated that the organisation 'would not use violent, brutal, inhuman or unlawful means'.

According to the applicants' submissions before the Court, the main activity of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden was the organisation of celebrations to commemorate historical events of importance for Macedonians in Bulgaria.
The United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden held a meeting for the first time on 22 April 1990 at the Rozhen Monastery, at the grave of Yane Sandanski.
On 20 April 1991 the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden organised a commemoration meeting at the Rozhen Monastery.
At the commemoration meeting of 20 April 1991 at the Rozhen Monastery, the participants adopted a declaration addressed to the President and Parliament of Bulgaria.

In July 1994 Mr Stankov, as chairman of the Petrich branch of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden, requested the mayor of Petrich to authorise a meeting to be held on 31 July 1994 in the area of Samuilova krepost in commemoration of a historical event.
Despite the refusal of the authorities, on 31 July 1994 some members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden attempted to approach the historical site of Samuilova krepost.
According to the applicants' assessment, approximately 120 to 150 members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden attempted to approach Samuilova krepost on 31 July 1994.

On 10 April 1995 the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden requested the mayor of Sandanski to authorise a meeting to be held on 22 April 1995 at the grave of Yane Sandanski at the Rozhen Monastery, on the occasion of the eightieth anniversary of his death.

The applicants submitted that a group of their supporters who had travelled to the Rozhen Monastery on 22 April 1995 had been ordered by the police to leave their cars in the nearby town of Melnik and had been transported to the monastery by local buses.
The applicants submitted that on 22 April 1995 their supporters had been allowed to visit the grave of Yane Sandanski at the Rozhen Monastery, to lay a wreath and to light candles.
The applicants submitted that on 22 April 1995 the participants celebrated the event without music, near the Rozhen Monastery but away from the grave.

In July 1995 the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden again requested authorisation to hold a commemorative meeting on 30 July 1995 at Samuilova krepost, the historical site in the vicinity of Petrich.

On 8 April 1997 the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden informed the mayor of Sandanski and the local police that they were organising a meeting to be held on 20 April 1997 at the Rozhen Monastery to commemorate the death of Yane Sandanski.
The applicants claimed that on 20 April 1997 the police had prevented a group of their supporters from approaching the Rozhen Monastery.

On 14 July 1997 Mr Stankov, as chairman of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden's branch in Petrich, requested authorisation for a commemorative meeting to be held on 2 August 1997 at Samuilova krepost, in the outskirts of Petrich.

The applicants submitted that on 2 August 1997 the police had not allowed a group of supporters of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden to reach the historical site of Samuilova krepost in the vicinity of Petrich.

The memorandum of 1 July 1997 stated that the signatories were not acting through confrontation, tension or violence, and that their way to achieve enjoyment of their rights as a Macedonian ethnic minority in Bulgaria and in Pirin Macedonia was through peaceful means and negotiations.
The 1998 police report stated that since 1992 the municipalities in the region had normally refused to allow events organised by the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden to proceed.
On 13 July 1994 the mayor of Petrich refused permission for the meeting requested by Mr Stankov, without giving any reasons.
The United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden appealed to the Petrich District Court against the mayor of Petrich's refusal of 13 July 1994.
The Petrich District Court dismissed the appeal on 16 July 1994.

The Petrich District Court found that since the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden had been banned, there were well-founded fears that the demonstration would endanger public order and the rights and freedoms of others.

On 28 July 1994 Mr Ivanov, the representative of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden, was issued with a written warning by the police to stay away from the official traditional fair at Samuilova krepost.
On 28 July 1994 another person (in addition to Mr Ivanov) was issued with a written warning by the police to stay away from the official traditional fair at Samuilova krepost.
The written warnings issued on 28 July 1994 stated that they were based on the applicable law.

On 31 July 1994 the police blocked the way of members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden attempting to approach Samuilova krepost; according to the applicants, the police were heavily armed.
On 14 April 1995 the mayor of Sandanski refused the request for a meeting on 22 April 1995, on the ground that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden was not duly registered by the courts.

On 15 April 1995 the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden appealed to the Sandanski District Court against the mayor of Sandanski's refusal, stating inter alia that the Macedonian people had been deprived of their right to their own cultural life in violation of international law.
The Sandanski District Court never examined the appeal lodged by the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden on 15 April 1995.

The legal requirements for the organisation of meetings are set out in the Bulgarian Meetings and Marches Act of 1990.
Section 2 of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that meetings and marches may be organised by individuals, associations, political or other public organisations.

Section 8(1) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that where a meeting is to be held outdoors the organisers shall notify in writing the respective People's Council or mayor's office not later than forty-eight hours before the beginning of the meeting, indicating the name of the organiser, the aim of the meeting, and the place and time of the meeting.
Section 9(1) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the organisers of the meeting shall take the measures necessary to ensure order during the event.

Section 12(1) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that where the time or place of the meeting, or the itinerary of the march, would create a situation endangering public order or traffic safety, the President of the Executive Committee of the People's Council or the mayor shall propose their modification.

Section 12(2) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the President of the Executive Committee of the People's Council or the mayor shall be competent to prohibit the holding of a meeting, demonstration or march where reliable information exists that it aims at the violent overturning of constitutional public order or is directed against the territorial integrity of the country, would endanger public order in the local community, or would breach the rights and freedoms of others.
Section 12(3) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the prohibition shall be imposed by a written reasoned act not later than twenty-four hours following the notification.

Section 12(4) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the organiser of the meeting, demonstration or march may appeal to the Executive Committee of the People's Council against the prohibition, and the Executive Committee shall decide within twenty-four hours.

Section 12(5) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that where the Executive Committee of the People's Council has not decided within the twenty-four hour time-limit, the march, demonstration or meeting may proceed.

Section 12(6) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that if the appeal is dismissed the dispute shall be referred to the relevant district court which shall decide within five days, and that court's decision shall be final.

The declaration adopted at the meeting of 20 April 1991 demanded the complete cultural, economic and political autonomy of Pirin Macedonia and the withdrawal of the Bulgarian occupation armies from Pirin Macedonia.

According to the 1998 police report, on 22 April 1990 a declaration requesting the recognition of a Macedonian minority and cultural autonomy had been read out.
The 1998 police report did not mention any incident at the meeting of 22 April 1990.

According to the 1998 police report, members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden, standing on a separate platform on 20 April 1991, had allegedly hissed and booed the police, labelled the Bulgarians 'barbarians', 'conquerors' and 'enslavers' and called on them to leave and 'free' the region from their presence.
